pattern.name: Calm 4-6
phase.in.label: Breathe in slowly
phase.out.label: Breathe out slowly
info.intro: A short, guided breathing practice. Follow the orb: it grows as you breathe in and settles as you breathe out. You don't need to read any of this to start — it will be here whenever you're curious.
info.how.heading: How it works
info.how.body:
The 4:6 rhythm makes every exhale longer than the inhale. That long, slow out-breath stimulates the vagus nerve — the main pathway of the parasympathetic nervous system — signalling the body to shift from "fight or flight" into "rest and repair".

The shift is measurable: heart rate slows, blood pressure eases, and circulation improves, bringing more oxygen to the brain. Practised regularly, it becomes a reliable lever you can pull whenever stress builds.
info.how.card1.title: Vagal nerve activation
info.how.card1.body: Slow, deep breathing stimulates the vagus nerve, which connects the brain to the heart and digestive system and promotes a calm state.
info.how.card2.title: Optimal gas exchange
info.how.card2.body: Breathing at 4–6 breaths per minute optimizes oxygen delivery and CO₂ balance, countering the shallow over-breathing that often comes with anxiety.
info.how.card3.title: Lower stress hormones
info.how.card3.body: Regular practice reduces cortisol and other stress hormones, improving the body's baseline stress response over time.
info.science.heading: The science
info.science.body: Research consistently shows that slow, diaphragmatic breathing produces measurable reductions in anxiety, stress hormones, and physiological arousal. In one controlled study, an 8-week program of 15-minute sessions lowered negative affect and significantly decreased cortisol levels in healthy adults.
info.science.card1.title: Anxiety reduction
info.science.card1.body: Five days of guided deep breathing (15–20 minutes, four times daily) reduced anxiety scores in hospitalized patients by 43%, while a control group showed no change.
info.science.card2.title: Panic disorder
info.science.card2.body: A review of 16 studies found that slow-breathing training over 2–12 months reduced panic attack frequency and normalized CO₂ levels in panic disorder and agoraphobia.
info.science.card3.title: Generalized anxiety
info.science.card3.body: Three months of daily breathing practice reduced anxiety scores by 68% in a study of 41 people with generalized anxiety disorder.

info.tips.heading: Tips for best results
info.tips.card1.title: Posture
info.tips.card1.body: Sit or stand tall so the lungs can expand fully. Keep the shoulders heavy and relaxed, not hunched.
info.tips.card2.title: Environment
info.tips.card2.body: Choose a quiet spot where you won't be interrupted. A comfortable temperature makes it easier to stay with the breath.
info.tips.card3.title: Consistency
info.tips.card3.body: Practice the same rhythm for a week before changing anything. Familiarity is what makes it work under real stress.
info.disclaimer: These exercises support everyday calm. They are not therapy and do not treat anxiety disorders or any medical condition. If a breathing exercise ever feels uncomfortable or makes you dizzy, stop and let your breath return to normal.
